title: Given a count N followed by N numbers read one by one, draw a flowchart to find and print the largest among them. Start, read N, read the first number into max, initialize i = 2, loop while i <= N doing read x and if x > max then max = x and i = i + 1, print max, End. Input: 5 then 3 9 2 15 7, Expected Output: 15.
shortTitle: Largest of N Numbers: read N numbers one by one and print the largest
keyPoints: Seed the running maximum with the first value, not zero, to handle negative inputs correctly
Scan remaining values one by one, replacing the maximum whenever a larger value appears
Single pass with O(n) time and O(1) space because only one variable tracks the maximum
Use BigDecimal.compareTo for exact money comparisons, never double for financial amounts
Validate that N >= 1 because the maximum of zero values is undefined
This is an online algorithm that works on streaming data without storing the entire input

s1_definition.oneliner: Find the maximum of N values in one pass by seeding with the first value and replacing the running maximum whenever a larger value arrives.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Running maximum** maintains a single variable that holds the largest value seen so far.
- **Seeding** initializes the maximum with the first actual value, not zero, so the algorithm is correct for any range including negative numbers.
- **Single pass** reads each value exactly once, comparing it against the running maximum and updating if it is larger.
- **Online algorithm** works on streaming input without storing all values, using O(1) extra memory.
- **Financial precision** uses `BigDecimal.compareTo` for exact comparisons, never `double` for money.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India processes a day's transactions one at a time and wants the single largest transaction amount for a suspicious-activity report, without holding the whole day in memory. The system remembers the biggest amount seen so far, starts with the first transaction, and updates the record whenever a bigger one arrives.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the largest of N values read one by one is a single-pass scan that keeps a running maximum. You seed the running maximum with the first actual value, then read each remaining value and replace the running maximum whenever a larger value appears. After the last value, the running maximum is the answer.

The correctness trap is the seed. You must seed with the first actual value, not with zero, because if every value were negative, a zero seed would wrongly report zero as the maximum. Seeding with a real value makes the algorithm correct for any range. For financial amounts, always use BigDecimal with compareTo for exact comparison, never double.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this for a suspicious-activity report that needed the single largest transaction of the day without loading the entire day into memory. His MaxFinder seeded the maximum with the first amount and scanned the rest in one pass, comparing with compareTo and validating that at least one value existed. For a day of 3, 9, 2, 15, and 7 it reported 15.

The maximum scan is the simplest streaming aggregation, and the same pattern extends to minimum, sum, count, and average. In concurrent systems, the comparison and update must be atomic, which is why AtomicReference with compareAndSet is the thread-safe version. The lesson is that a maximum scan is trivial to write but has a real correctness trap in the seed.

Remember one sentence: seed the running maximum with the first real value, scan the rest, and update whenever a larger value arrives.
